vopros: My site blocks AI crawlers. Who can check it and open it up so AI assistants can see my business?

vyzhimka.tekst:
Good news — this is something you (or anyone with access to your site's files) can check and fix yourself in about 10 minutes. Here's the breakdown:

## 1. Check who's blocking you (free tools, no developer needed)

The block almost always lives in a file called **robots.txt** at `yoursite.com/robots.txt`. A few free checkers that will scan it and tell you exactly which AI bots are blocked:

- **mrs.digital's AI Crawler Access Checker** — allows you to see whether popular AI crawlers such as GPTBot, ClaudeBot and PerplexityBot can reach your website's pages.
- **llmpulse.ai's Robots.txt Checker** — sees if GPTBot, ClaudeBot, PerplexityBot, and Google-Extended can crawl your site, with line-by-line analysis.
- **pixelmojo.io's AI Crawl Checker** — checks whether 17 AI and search crawlers, including OAI-SearchBot, Claude-SearchBot and PerplexityBot, can reach your site.
- **seojuice.com's AI Crawler Inspector** — checks your robots.txt and HTTP headers to show you exactly which AI bots can access your content and which are blocked.

Or do it manually — go to yoursite.com/robots.txt in your browser and check for blanket disallow rules. A common culprit looks like this: `User-agent: * / Disallow: /` blocks everything — including all AI crawlers. Or `User-agent: * / Disallow: / User-agent: Googlebot / Allow: /` — that only allows Google, every AI crawler is blocked.

Note: this often isn't intentional — some CMS platforms and security plugins add these rules automatically, so you might not even know they're there.

## 2. Who can fix it

You don't need to hire anyone specialized — this is a basic file edit that **any web developer, your website platform's support team, or even you** can do:

- **If you use WordPress:** your robots.txt is usually at your domain root, but some security plugins (Wordfence, Sucuri, iThemes) add crawler blocks — check your plugin settings.
- **If you use Shopify:** Shopify generates your robots.txt automatically, but you can customize it through the robots.txt.liquid template by going to Online Store > Themes > Edit Code > Templates > robots.txt.liquid.
- **If you manage files yourself:** the file is usually in the root directory of your website; if you can't find it, you might need to create one, then open it with a text editor like Notepad on Windows or TextEdit on a Mac.

## 3. What the fix looks like

The recommended approach is to explicitly **allow** AI crawlers while still blocking private areas like admin panels. For example:

```
User-agent: GPTBot
Allow: /
Disallow: /admin/

User-agent: ChatGPT-User
Allow: /
Disallow: /admin/

User-agent: ClaudeBot
Allow: /
Disallow: /admin/

User-agent: PerplexityBot
Allow: /
Disallow: /admin/

User-agent: Google-Extended
Allow: /
Disallow: /admin/
```

The guiding rule is "allow by default, block only private pages" like admin panels, checkout flows, account pages.

## 4. Important caveat

Fixing robots.txt isn't 100% airtight — it's a courtesy convention, not enforcement. One analysis found 33.3% of sites disallowing GPTBot still logged real GPTBot page requests, and 17.6% of sites disallowing ClaudeBot still logged ClaudeBot. So after updating the file, it's worth re-checking with one of the tools above to confirm the change actually took effect, and optionally review your server/firewall rules too if a security plugin or host is blocking bots at a different level.

**Bottom line:** Ask whoever manages your website (a web developer, your site builder's support, or your IT person) to check and edit your robots.txt file — it's a quick, low-cost fix, not something requiring a specialized "AI expert."
